prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, providing the theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed since round 1. I now put B002, with Kiyotaki and Moore alone, ahead of B025, which I preferred at opening. The change rests on three points. First, attribution. Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a two-author founding paper with no obvious missing originator. For B025, the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum was raised by Fredriksson, Hassler, Hjalmarsson, Krusell and Stromberg, and Dreber conceded it. I had treated this gap as a caveat, but the exchange persuaded me that it is a real obstacle to a clean Helpman-Melitz citation. The exporter-heterogeneity regularities and parts of the theory were developed by people the ballot cannot credit. Second, overlap. Boppart's argument that the 2022 prize concerned banks, runs and intermediation, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral values feeding back on credit and asset prices over time, is persuasive to me as a distinction of mechanism. I make the same distinction for Melitz selection against Krugman 2008, but there the credit gap compounds it. Third, maturity and reach. The mechanism has about three decades of use in theory, quantitative macro and policy modelling, and its relevance was tested by 2008. I do not rely on the number of members who prefer B002. That count is not scientific merit, and I note that the chair's summary shows no configuration reaching six explicit supporters. My reasons are credit clarity, originality of the mechanism and durability. I keep B025 as my first alternative because the selection-and-reallocation mechanism and the firm-level confirmation are strong. I would support it if the Committee judged the Bernard et al. gap tolerable. On Gertler, I stop at two names. His credit is split with B043, the accelerator lineage runs through Bernanke and Gilchrist, and the cap of three people argues for a bounded citation. I do not combine B002 with a Melitz-only B025 part. Dropping Helpman would misstate that contribution, and a prize pairing macro-finance with trade has no common theme.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. Several members, including Boppart, Dreber, Enflo and Hjalmarsson, note that the size of collateral-driven amplification is identified less cleanly than the theory's influence suggests. B025 has a longer record of firm-level tests of its core predictions, which I weighted heavily at opening. I have not changed my view that this favours B025. I have only judged that clarity of credit and the distinctness of the mechanism outweigh it. A second reservation is that the 2022 prize may be read as having covered neighbouring ground. I cannot settle that from the supplied materials, and it remains a judgment for the Committee. A third is that a two-name credit leaves the accelerator strand (Gertler, Gilchrist) unrecognised, and Hassler sees that as a narrower citation than the literature warrants. My field is international pricing, trade and IO. That made me more receptive to B025 and B012 at opening and now makes me look hard at whether I am discounting that bias correctly. Leaving my first choice might reflect overcorrection toward the crowd.

responses.point: Hassler prefers Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler for B002. He argues that Gertler's later intermediary-based quantitative work, including with Kiyotaki and Karadi, is separable from the 2022 recognition. He accepts Kiyotaki and Moore alone as a fallback.
responses.response: I take the chair's question about what separates Gertler's intermediary work from the 2022 prize seriously. From the supplied material I can say only that the distinction is plausible, since banks, runs and crisis analysis differ from quantitative models of intermediary balance sheets. I cannot verify how that literature divides credit. Even if the separation holds, I still prefer two names. Gertler's credit is also claimed under the eight-name B043. A citation written around financial frictions in propagation would be a broader prize than the collateral-constraint originating contribution, and it would reopen the Gilchrist question. I welcome your fallback. If the Committee preferred a broader financial-frictions citation, I would want that to be debated as a different prize.

responses.point: Boppart keeps B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues that the 2022 prize concerned banks, runs and intermediation, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral values creating a dynamic feedback loop, so the overlap is thematic and not a duplication of the discovery.
responses.response: This distinction moved my ordering. I apply the same principle consistently: adjacency to a recent prize is a balance consideration for the Committee, not a merit demerit, when the mechanism and its empirical implications differ. By that principle B025 is also separable from Krugman 2008. The difference between B002 and B025 is therefore not overlap. It is that B002 has a clean two-author origin and B025 has a credit gap that the ballot cannot close. I share your reservation about direct empirical identification of the amplification magnitude, and I did not resolve it. You and Dreber both stress it, and it is the main reason this is not an easy switch for me.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B025 first and B002 second. She values the sustained firm-level confirmation of Melitz-style predictions and concedes that the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is an attribution risk the ballot's names cannot resolve. She treats B002 as a serious competitor.
responses.response: Your concession is part of why I moved. I agree with your assessment of the evidence behind B025, and I opened with the same view. I do not claim that the empirical record for collateral amplification matches it. Where we may differ is how to weigh a conceptual origin with a clean credit against a better-confirmed framework whose credit gap cannot be fixed within the list. In answer to the chair's question, I now place B002 above B025 because of that gap. I would accept B025 as a reasonable choice if the Committee judged the gap manageable. I think we both treat the other as a legitimate prize, and I would not describe the choice as clear-cut.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B012 first and names B002 as her main fallback. She stresses that BLP demand estimation is a measurement framework with economic content (markups, substitution, welfare), and she wants a citation worded narrowly enough that it does not imply credit for all of empirical IO.
responses.response: I accept that BLP is more than a statistical device, and I said in round 1 that I would not oppose B012 if the Committee preferred a methods-based prize. I keep it as my second alternative. My ordering still gives B002 an edge, for two reasons. B012's credit set is seven names, and as you noted, if Bresnahan were judged equal in kind, no three-person set would be fully defensible. B002 has no comparable problem. I also see that you name B002 as your fallback. I do not read that as evidence of merit, but it does suggest that the two-author collateral mechanism has the cleanest credit among the leading candidates.

responses.point: Teorell proposes a two-part configuration, B002 for Kiyotaki and Moore and B012 for Pakes alone, and he accepts that Berry and Levinsohn are a real attribution loss. He calls B002 with Gertler his single-part fallback.
responses.response: I considered a two-part configuration and did not adopt it. Your own conflict note admits that a prize joining macro-finance with empirical IO has no obvious common theme, and that Pakes-alone omits Berry and Levinsohn from BLP. I would not accept that attribution cost in order to fit the cap of three people. I agree with you on dropping Gertler from B002. In answer to the chair's question, I would support B002 with Kiyotaki and Moore alone as a single part, and I would not support the two-part version.

uncertainties: Whether the 2022 prize on banks, runs and financial crises covers the collateral-constraint mechanism enough to weaken B002. I treat it as thematic overlap, but I cannot settle it from the supplied evidence.
How much weight the Committee should place on the weaker empirical identification of collateral amplification relative to the firm-level confirmation behind B025.
Whether the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is disqualifying for B025. I now treat it as decisive between B002 and B025 for me, but I have not verified relative credit independently.
Whether my move toward B002 overcorrects for field affinity, or follows the room too closely.
Whether a financial-frictions citation including Gertler would be a defensible broader alternative. I treat it as a different prize and have not adjudicated the credit split with B043.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific connection is apparent from the supplied profile. None of my listed co-authors (Asplund, Steen, Ulsaker, Grönqvist, Wilander, Syverson, Goldstein) is a credited name on the shortlisted ballots. I co-authored a 2026 paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen, neither of whom is a candidate. Hassler is the only member whose preferred B002 part includes Gertler, and I have now moved toward B002, though to the two-name version he accepts as a fallback. I disclose this without adjudicating it, and I state that my reasons for the change are the ones given above. My research on exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency and cross-border pricing is adjacent to B025 and B012, and my preferred part is now outside that adjacency. My spouse, Magdalena Andersson, is a public fact and there is no evidence it bears on these candidates. I do not treat it as a conflict.
